questions.topic: The Contrastive Training Objective
questions.question: What does contrastive retrieval training encourage?
options: Positive pairs to score above the competing documents in the batch
Every document vector to spread evenly across the unit sphere
Query and document towers to converge on identical parameters
Scores to fall within a fixed range so thresholds transfer

questions.topic: The Contrastive Training Objective
questions.question: What does temperature control in a contrastive softmax?
options: How many negatives contribute to each example's loss term
How sharply the loss distinguishes between competing scores
How quickly the learning rate decays across training steps
How much the positive score is offset before normalization

questions.topic: The Contrastive Training Objective
questions.question: A hard negative receives nearly the positive score. What happens to the loss signal?
options: It vanishes, because the two scores nearly cancel in the softmax
It saturates, because the softmax is already close to its maximum
It strengthens, because the positive becomes less probable
It inverts, because the negative is treated as the ranked winner

questions.topic: The Contrastive Training Objective
questions.question: Why do false negatives damage contrastive training?
options: They unbalance the batch, so the softmax normalizes inconsistently
They inflate the measured loss without changing any gradient
They slow convergence by adding examples the model already fits
They push genuinely relevant pairs apart in the learned space

questions.topic: The Contrastive Training Objective
questions.question: Which split most directly reduces near-duplicate leakage?
options: Hold out complete document families, or a later time period
Deduplicate by exact hash before assigning examples to splits
Stratify the split so each contains the same topic distribution
Assign each near-duplicate cluster randomly, one chunk at a time

questions.topic: The Contrastive Training Objective
questions.question: Why is the learned geometry task-dependent?
options: The pooling strategy decides which token evidence survives training
Positive and negative sampling define which distinctions matter
The similarity metric determines how the space is shaped during training
The corpus vocabulary fixes which directions the model can express

questions.topic: In-Batch Negatives vs Hard Negative Mining
questions.question: What is an in-batch negative?
options: A passage sampled uniformly from the corpus for each query
A passage the previous checkpoint scored below the current positive
Another pair's positive, reused as a negative for this query
A passage generated by perturbing the positive's text

questions.topic: In-Batch Negatives vs Hard Negative Mining
questions.question: What is a hard negative?
options: A passage that appears in many queries' candidate sets at once
A passage whose vector norm is unusually large for the corpus
A passage from a domain the model has never been trained on
A plausible, high-scoring passage that is judged nonrelevant

questions.topic: In-Batch Negatives vs Hard Negative Mining
questions.question: Why are in-batch negatives computationally efficient?
options: One score matrix over the batch supplies every comparison
Negatives are reused across steps, so encoding happens once
They require no backward pass, since their labels are implicit
They are sampled offline, so training does no extra encoding

questions.topic: In-Batch Negatives vs Hard Negative Mining
questions.question: Why can random negatives stop improving a trained model?
options: They shrink the effective batch size as training progresses
Most become too easy, so they contribute little useful gradient
They drift toward the positives as the space becomes anisotropic
They over-represent frequent documents once the corpus grows

questions.topic: In-Batch Negatives vs Hard Negative Mining
questions.question: Mined negatives contain many unlabeled valid answers. What should the team do?
options: Lower the mining threshold so fewer near-positives are captured
Keep them, since contrastive loss is robust to a small label error rate
Filter known positives and review the quality of the mining step
Re-label the mined set as positives, since the model scored them highly

questions.topic: In-Batch Negatives vs Hard Negative Mining
questions.question: Why refresh hard negatives as the model improves?
options: The mining index drifts out of sync with the serving index
Stale negatives accumulate label noise as judgments are revised
Batch composition must change to keep the softmax well conditioned
Candidates that were once difficult may no longer challenge the model

questions.topic: Fine-Tuning an Embedder on Domain Data
questions.question: What should domain fine-tuning examples reflect?
options: Production queries, documents, languages and relevance judgments
The public benchmarks the base model was originally evaluated on
The longest and most information-dense documents in the corpus
Query-document pairs the current system already ranks correctly

questions.topic: Fine-Tuning an Embedder on Domain Data
questions.question: What is catastrophic forgetting?
options: Training diverges and the checkpoint can no longer be recovered
Adaptation degrades capabilities the model had previously learned
The optimizer state is discarded, so training cannot be resumed
Old vectors become unreadable once the tokenizer is replaced

questions.topic: Fine-Tuning an Embedder on Domain Data
questions.question: Why compare against the full production hybrid system?
options: Dense metrics and lexical metrics are computed on different corpora
Hybrid fusion weights have to be retrained whenever a tower changes
A gain in the model may not improve the complete retrieval funnel
Offline judgments are only valid when measured after reranking

questions.topic: Fine-Tuning an Embedder on Domain Data
questions.question: What must accompany a fine-tuned encoder release?
options: A retuned approximate index, since recall curves shift with the model
A refreshed set of hard negatives mined against the new checkpoint
An updated fusion weight so lexical and dense scores stay comparable
Compatible re-embedding and a versioned index migration

questions.topic: Fine-Tuning an Embedder on Domain Data
questions.question: Overall recall rises while multilingual recall collapses. What is the strongest decision process?
options: Weigh each segment's requirements and traffic before deciding to deploy
Deploy, then fine-tune a second checkpoint for the multilingual segment
Roll back, since a regression in any segment blocks the release
Re-weight the aggregate metric so segments contribute proportionally

questions.topic: Fine-Tuning an Embedder on Domain Data
questions.question: Which artifact set makes a fine-tuning result reproducible?
options: The checkpoint, its training loss curve and the evaluation harness
Data, model, tokenizer, instructions, pooling and length settings
The training data snapshot and the random seed used for sampling
The base model version and the hyperparameters that were swept

questions.topic: MTEB and Instruction-Tuned Embedding Models
questions.question: What does MTEB provide?
options: A reference implementation for serving embeddings at scale
A standard training corpus for contrastive retrieval models
Comparative embedding evaluations across many tasks and datasets
A certification that a model is safe for production retrieval use

questions.topic: MTEB and Instruction-Tuned Embedding Models
questions.question: What is an instruction-tuned embedder designed to consume?
options: A schema describing the fields present in each document
A similarity threshold supplied alongside every query
A separate codebook for queries and for documents
A task or role instruction alongside the text itself

questions.topic: MTEB and Instruction-Tuned Embedding Models
questions.question: Why is an aggregate leaderboard score insufficient?
options: Target task, language, latency, cost and licensing all differ
Leaderboards average over datasets with inconsistent label quality
Aggregate scores are computed before any approximate indexing
Public benchmarks are saturated, so the ranking is mostly noise

questions.topic: MTEB and Instruction-Tuned Embedding Models
questions.question: Why must required query prefixes be preserved in serving?
options: The prefix is hashed into the vector ID the index stores
The model was trained to separate roles using that exact formatting
The prefix carries the tenant identity the filter depends on
Dropping it changes the token count and so the pooled length

questions.topic: MTEB and Instruction-Tuned Embedding Models
questions.question: Model A gains one recall point but doubles memory and misses the latency objective. Which choice is strongest?
options: Take A and recover the latency by lowering the index's probe count
Take A and shard further, since memory is the cheaper constraint
Take the cheaper model, provided it meets every quality floor
Take A only for the query segments where the recall gain appears

questions.topic: MTEB and Instruction-Tuned Embedding Models
questions.question: How should a team validate a leaderboard shortlist?
options: Reproduce the leaderboard numbers on the published evaluation sets
Compare the models' training corpora against the production domain
Measure each model's throughput and memory under production load
Run held-out production-like queries through the full pipeline

questions.topic: Matryoshka Embeddings: Truncatable Dimensions
questions.question: What makes a Matryoshka embedding truncatable?
options: Training makes each leading prefix of the vector independently useful
Dimensions are ordered by variance once training has finished
The model emits several vectors and the shortest is stored
A projection matrix maps the full vector down on demand

questions.topic: Matryoshka Embeddings: Truncatable Dimensions
questions.question: What is a main benefit of a shorter supported prefix?
options: It sharpens the distinction between near neighbours
It cuts vector memory and the work done per comparison
It makes the index tolerant of encoder version changes
It reduces the number of graph edges the index must store

questions.topic: Matryoshka Embeddings: Truncatable Dimensions
questions.question: Why not truncate an arbitrary embedding model?
options: Its similarity metric would have to be recalibrated after cutting
Truncation breaks normalization, so cosine becomes ill-defined
Useful information is not guaranteed to concentrate in the prefix
Most models order dimensions by frequency, not by importance

questions.topic: Matryoshka Embeddings: Truncatable Dimensions
questions.question: What must match between query and document vectors?
options: The batch size used when each side was originally encoded
The instruction prefix applied to both sides of the pair
The corpus statistics used to normalize each side's scores
The selected prefix dimension and the preprocessing applied

questions.topic: Matryoshka Embeddings: Truncatable Dimensions
questions.question: A 384-dimension prefix meets every quality floor while 768 adds little gain. What is the best judgment?
options: Take 384, provided the measured system savings are worth having
Take 768, since the headroom protects against future corpus growth
Take 384 for storage but query at 768 to preserve ranking quality
Take whichever the approximate index reports higher recall on

questions.topic: Matryoshka Embeddings: Truncatable Dimensions
questions.question: Why rebuild the ANN benchmark after truncation?
options: Truncated vectors must be re-normalized before they can be indexed
Lower dimensions change the index's recall and latency behaviour
The exact baseline is only valid at the model's full dimension
Truncation alters the metric, so old measurements are incomparable

questions.topic: Scalar and Binary Quantization: Recall per Dollar
questions.question: What does scalar quantization reduce?
options: The number of dimensions retained in each stored vector
The number of candidates the index examines per query
The numeric precision used for each vector coordinate
The number of codebooks the index has to keep resident

questions.topic: Scalar and Binary Quantization: Recall per Dollar
questions.question: What does sign-based binary quantization store per dimension?
options: A four-byte float, rounded toward the nearest codeword
A one-byte integer, scaled to the observed value range
A two-bit code covering the sign and one magnitude bucket
A single bit

questions.topic: Scalar and Binary Quantization: Recall per Dollar
questions.question: What can outliers do to scalar calibration?
options: They widen the range and waste resolution on common values
They shift the mean, so quantized vectors lose their normalization
They dominate the distance computation once values are clipped
They force a larger codebook, cancelling the memory saving

questions.topic: Scalar and Binary Quantization: Recall per Dollar
questions.question: How can full-precision vectors complement binary candidates?
options: They calibrate the quantization ranges as the corpus distribution drifts
They rerank a shortlist to recover the ordering quality that was lost
They serve the queries whose filters leave too few binary candidates
They provide the ground truth the binary recall is measured against

questions.topic: Scalar and Binary Quantization: Recall per Dollar
questions.question: Why can truncation plus quantization hurt more than either alone?
options: Both are applied at index time, so neither can be tuned afterwards
Truncation invalidates the calibration ranges quantization depends on
Dimension loss and precision error compound in the same comparison
The shortlist shrinks twice, so reranking has too little to work with

questions.topic: Scalar and Binary Quantization: Recall per Dollar
questions.question: Which measurement best represents recall per dollar?
options: Stored bytes per vector against recall at a fixed probe setting
Recall against the exact baseline, divided by peak index memory
Throughput per replica at the recall the quality floor requires
End-to-end quality, latency, memory, replicas and reranking cost
